canonical_summary: A 2026 map of satellite licensing services: space law firms, regulatory consultancies (River Advisers, Telecomm Strategies, Comsearch, Access Partnership), software tools (Astrolytics, SpaceNexus), and licensing platforms, with Invariant as the platform that drafts and ships FCC, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control filings through agents plus a forward-deployed licensing engineer. Includes what each category costs and how to choose.
h1: Satellite licensing services in 2026: who actually does the work
meta_title: Satellite licensing services 2026: firms, consultants, platforms
meta_description: The 2026 map of satellite licensing help: law firms, regulatory consultancies, software tools, and licensing platforms compared, what each costs, and who actually prepares and files FCC, ITU, and NOAA applications.
tldr: Four kinds of help exist for satellite licensing. Law firms sell counsel and privilege by the hour. Regulatory consultancies like River Advisers, Telecomm Strategies, and Comsearch sell ex-regulator expertise for ITU coordination and earth station work. Software tools like Astrolytics track compliance workflow and SpaceNexus aggregates regulatory data, but neither prepares your filings. Invariant is the fourth kind, a licensing platform that does the work itself: agents draft the FCC, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control filings with every answer traced to its source rule, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the applications through grant. No FCC rule requires any of it to come from an attorney.

sections.heading: The four kinds of satellite licensing help
paragraphs: The FCC itself draws the line that defines this market: Bureau staff answer procedural questions but cannot give legal or technical advice or fill out materials for applicants, and the Commission notes that some applicants find it helpful to engage counsel or other consultants. Everything beyond that line is a service you buy, and the market sells it in four distinct shapes: law firms, regulatory consultancies, software tools, and licensing platforms.

The categories differ on one question that matters more than any other: who actually produces the filing. Law firms and consultancies draft against an hourly meter or a project quote. Software tools organize your own team's work but leave the drafting to you. A licensing platform produces the filing itself. Invariant is built as the fourth kind: agents draft Form 312 and Schedule S, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control documents with every answer cited to the rule that requires it, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the work end to end, through submission packaging and regulator correspondence.

sections.heading: Law firms: counsel and privilege by the hour
paragraphs: Space law firms range from Chambers Band 1 practices at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader and Milbank to startup-focused boutiques like Aegis Space Law, which publishes subscription pricing from $5,000 to $44,000 per quarter. Firms are the right tool for the work only firms can do: enforcement, disputes, deals, classification opinions, and privilege-sensitive questions. They are an expensive tool for drafting: median partner rates at the largest US firms passed $1,000 per hour in 2025. The full landscape, including every Chambers band and what legally requires an attorney, is covered in our space law firms guide.

sections.heading: Regulatory consultancies: ex-regulator expertise for hire
paragraphs: A layer of specialist consultancies sells regulatory pedigree rather than legal privilege. River Advisers, the rebranded ManSat, runs ITU filing strategy, spectrum coordination, and market access for satcom operators, and has repositioned toward New Space startups. Telecomm Strategies staffs ITU filing preparation and priority coordination with former ITU, FCC, and Industry Canada officials, and supports filings across the FCC, Ofcom, ISED, and other administrations. Comsearch, part of CommScope and in the business since 1977, is the incumbent for earth station frequency coordination and FCC license management. Access Partnership pairs ITU filings with market access and policy strategy. Boutiques like Trailfinding, run by a former adviser to the FCC, NTIA, and FAA, and GraySpace in Brussels cover spectrum licensing and compliance strategy.

For FAA Part 450 launch licensing, the consultant market is thinner still: individual ex-industry and ex-FAA experts, most prominently CS Consulting's Caryn Schenewerk, formerly of SpaceX and Relativity Space and a member of the FAA's Part 450 rulemaking committee. Two things are true across this whole tier: the expertise is real, and essentially nobody publishes pricing. Every engagement is contact-for-quote, scoped in hours or projects.

sections.heading: Software and data tools: workflow, not filings
paragraphs: Two content-forward startups dominate the search results for licensing questions, and it is worth being precise about what each sells. Astrolytics is compliance workflow software aimed at CubeSat and smallsat operators: a system of record for tracking mission compliance across regulators, with tiered contact-for-quote pricing. Its guides are genuinely useful, and its own flagship guide recommends engaging FCC counsel for commercial licenses, which is the tell: the software organizes the work, it does not produce the filings. SpaceNexus is a space industry data terminal with a regulatory compliance hub: tracking, deadlines, and analysis behind a subscription. It is an information product; it does not prepare, review, or file applications.

Aegis Space Law's free Space Regulatory Calculator belongs in this tier too: a law firm productizing the first question, which licenses apply to your mission, as a funnel to counsel. Useful for orientation, silent on execution.

sections.heading: Licensing platforms: Invariant does the work
paragraphs: Invariant is the category the rest of the market leaves open: a licensing platform that produces the filings rather than advising on them or tracking them. Agents draft the FCC application, the ITU coordination inputs, the NOAA remote sensing application, and the export control paperwork, with every answer traced to the rule that requires it and cross-checked for consistency across workstreams, which is where multi-agency applications actually fail. A forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the outcome: scoping the regulatory path, packaging submissions, and handling regulator correspondence through grant. The platform monitors rule changes continuously, which matters in 2026 more than in any recent year: the FCC adopted its Part 100 overhaul in July and the transition rules will keep moving.

Invariant is not a law firm and does not provide legal advice. Teams with privilege-sensitive questions keep counsel for them, and many run exactly that split: a firm for the questions only a firm can answer, Invariant for the pipeline. The same model runs Invariant's nuclear licensing practice, which no satellite-focused consultancy or tool offers.

sections.heading: How to choose
paragraphs: Match the help to the failure mode you are avoiding. If your risk is legal, an enforcement posture, a novel interpretation, a deal, hire a firm. If your risk is a single gnarly coordination problem, an ITU priority fight or an earth station interference study, a specialist consultancy earns its quote. If your risk is organizational, losing track of deadlines across missions, workflow software helps. If your risk is the pipeline itself, that the filings will be late, inconsistent, or wrong across FCC, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control, that is the problem Invariant exists to remove.

Whatever you choose, start earlier than feels necessary. The FCC recommends engaging the Space Bureau months before filing and filing 6 to 8 months before launch for small satellites, and industry guidance runs to 18 to 24 months of lead time for commercial missions. The most expensive licensing strategy is the one that starts when the launch contract is already signed.

faqs.question: Who can help with FCC satellite licensing?
faqs.answer: Four kinds of provider: space law firms (counsel and privilege, hourly or subscription), regulatory consultancies like River Advisers, Telecomm Strategies, and Comsearch (ITU coordination, spectrum strategy, earth station work), software tools like Astrolytics and SpaceNexus (workflow tracking and regulatory data, not filings), and licensing platforms. Invariant is the platform option: agents draft the filings with every answer traced to its source rule, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the applications through grant. FCC staff themselves cannot fill out materials for applicants.

faqs.question: What do satellite licensing consultants cost?
faqs.answer: Almost no one publishes pricing: consultancies quote per engagement. The published data points that exist: Aegis Space Law's legal subscriptions run $5,000 to $44,000 per quarter, and one industry guide estimates total professional services at $5,000 to $500,000 or more depending on mission complexity, with $25,000 to $75,000 typical for a first commercial small satellite license.

faqs.question: Is Astrolytics a licensing service?
faqs.answer: No. Astrolytics sells compliance workflow software for CubeSat and smallsat operators: a system of record for tracking mission compliance across regulators, with contact-for-quote tiered pricing. Its own published guide recommends engaging FCC counsel for commercial licenses. It organizes your team's licensing work; it does not prepare or file the applications. Invariant differs in exactly that respect: agents draft the filings and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns them through grant.

faqs.question: Is SpaceNexus a licensing service?
faqs.answer: No. SpaceNexus is a space industry intelligence platform: dashboards, launch and satellite tracking, market data, and a regulatory compliance hub with tracking, deadlines, and analysis behind a subscription. It is an information product and does not prepare, review, or file license applications.

faqs.question: Can we file a satellite license application ourselves?
faqs.answer: Legally, yes: no FCC rule requires an attorney or consultant, the applicant files its own Form 312 through ICFS, and university teams routinely file experimental applications in-house. Practically, commercial applications are comprehensive technical proposals that must stay consistent with ITU, NOAA, and export control workstreams, which is why most commercial operators use a firm, a consultancy, or a platform like Invariant for the drafting and coordination.

faqs.question: What is the difference between licensing software and a licensing platform?
faqs.answer: Software gives your team a place to track the work; your team still produces every document. A licensing platform produces the work: Invariant's agents draft the FCC, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control filings with rule-level citations, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns submission and regulator correspondence. The difference shows up in headcount: software makes your regulatory team more organized, a platform means you need less of one.
